summary:
Maymar to mars is a 3D scientific Mars survival and orbital ascent simulation developed in Godot 4. Following a catastrophic crash-landing on the Martian surface, players navigate a seamless, procedurally generated spherical planet to secure habitat shelter, stabilize critical life support, and engineer an escape back to orbit.

our goal was to create a fun game which whould actual help kids learn gravity and what whouldhappenif a mission fails
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Mahmar To MARS puts you in the boots of an astronaut who has just crash-landed on Mars. You wake up battered, face-down in the red regolith, with your habitat in ruins and your ascent rocket offline. Your immediate goal is simple: stay alive and figure out how to get off the planet.

The whole game takes place on an authentic, seamless, spherical planet where gravity pulls you toward the world's center. There are no flat maps or invisible walls—you can literally run or jetpack all the way around the curvature of the planet and end up back where you started. To escape back to orbit, you have to repair the Mars Ascent Vehicle (MAV). But the rocket won’t clear for launch until you restore your base's three core life support systems:

  1. The Oxygen Scrubber: Requires you to brave the edge of a deep crevasse to salvage a replacement filter core.
  2. The Solar Power Unit: Demands a trek out to an abandoned rover half-buried in the dust to recover its power core.
  3. The Water System: Requires hiking up a mountain ridge to harvest raw cryogenic water ice from an ancient glacial basin.

Every system is tied together in real time: as the sun moves across the sky over a 10-minute sol, your solar panels generate power based on the sun's angle. If night falls or a dust storm blows in, power drops; if power hits zero, your oxygen scrubber stops and suit oxygen drains twice as fast; and if you burn your jetpack thrusters recklessly, your suit consumes three times more oxygen.

How is the project creative? (Our Outer Wilds Inspiration!)

We are massive fans of Mobius Digital's Outer Wilds, and it was the core inspiration behind this entire project!

Most traditional space survival games rely on flat, repetitive grid maps, tedious inventory crafting menus, and artificial grind. We wanted that unforgettable Outer Wilds feeling: the awe of standing on the curved horizon of a miniature planet, gazing up at a starry sky, firing your jetpack thrusters, and having the environment itself tell the story through physics and organic discovery.

We took that sense of wonder and paired it directly with authentic aerospace science. Instead of fantasy space magic, everything is grounded in real Martian realities:

  • Real-time Space Weather: We wired the game into NASA's live DONKI API. When a real Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) solar storm occurs, sirens blare across the surface, radiation spikes, and you have 30 seconds of pure adrenaline to hustle back to the safety of the Life Pod.
  • MOLA Martian Topography: The crater depth-to-radius ratios, the Noctis Labyrinthus chasm cracks, and the volcanic lava tube caves are all modeled after real Mars laser altimetry data from NASA's Mars Global Surveyor.
  • NASA Relics: Scattered across crater rims are historical relics from missions like Mariner 4, Viking 1, Sojourner, Opportunity, and Curiosity waiting to be discovered.

What benefits does it have and what is the intended impact?

We designed this as a children’s and students' educational experience that doesn't feel like a lecture.

You don't truly understand how delicate human survival is in deep space by reading a diagram in a textbook. You understand it when your suit's oxygen alarm is beeping at you because you got greedy with your jetpack, or when night falls and you realize your habitat batteries won't make it to sunrise unless you conserve power.

By turning closed-loop life support, orbital mechanics, and radiation shielding into active, hands-on gameplay decisions, we hope to spark genuine curiosity in kids and future engineers about what it will actually take to colonize the Red Planet.

What tools, software, and hardware did we use?

  • Game Engine: Godot 4.3+ with Jolt Physics 3D for rock-solid spherical collision detection and planetary gravity.
  • Language: GDScript for modular state machines, celestial orbits, and survival loops.
  • Shaders: Custom Godot shaders for Martian atmospheric scattering, procedural triplanar rock-sand blending, starry skies, and translucent ice basins.
  • Models & Art: Blender for 3D asset optimization and collision mesh generation; open-source sci-fi habitat and rover models; custom-rigged astronaut with procedural limp, lean, and prone-recovery animations.
  • APIs & Data: NASA Open APIs (specifically the Space Weather DONKI API) and MOLA planetary altimetry models.
  • Audio: Custom multi-channel audio featuring looping rocket engine audio, ambient Martian winds, and atmospheric entry rumble.
  • Hardware: Standard developer laptops running Windows 11 with Vulkan/DirectX 12 graphics.

What factors did our team consider?

  1. Accessibility vs. Scientific Realism: Orbital physics and closed-loop life support can easily get overwhelmingly complex. We worked hard to balance authentic science (solar elevation curves, cryogenic phase change, radiation decay) with responsive, fun arcade controls so that a 10-year-old can grab a keyboard or controller and immediately know what to do.
  2. Atmosphere & Emotional Tone: Surviving on Mars should feel lonely and dangerous, but never hopeless. We introduced a minimalist, clean HUD that hides when vitals are safe, subtle camera sway to simulate suit breathing, a wounded limp when you first crawl out of the crash, and an epic retro-burn rocket ascent at the end that pulls back to reveal the entire glowing red planet floating in the stars.
